tagline: River canyon, fossil country and former rail towns between Biggs and Baker City.
intro: Journey Through Time runs 286 miles from Biggs to Baker City, passing farming communities, river canyon and Blue Mountain foothills. ODOT gives a minimum driving time of eight to ten hours and presents the route as a journey through fossil beds and the towns of Oregon’s settlement era. Oregon designated it a State Scenic Byway in 1997.

The byway joins portions of five numbered highways, while older wagon and rail routes explain several towns along the drive. Antelope began as a station on the wagon road linking The Dalles with gold mines near Canyon City. In 1900, the Columbia Southern Railway reached Shaniko from Biggs, making Shaniko a regional shipping hub. A competing route through the Deschutes canyon diverted traffic in 1911, and Shaniko declined.

From Biggs, travel south through Moro and Shaniko, then east through Antelope toward Clarno’s fossil beds and Fossil. At Service Creek, the route joins the John Day River, following it for the next 100 miles through Spray and toward Dayville. Between Kimberly and Dayville, rimrock flanks the road above the river. Continue through John Day and Prairie City to Austin Junction, where OR 7 carries the journey east toward Baker City. The final approach descends gradually into Baker City’s historic downtown.

moments.title: Shaniko
moments.text: A rail terminus made Shaniko a wool-shipping center in the first decade of the twentieth century. The Columbia Southern branch from Biggs arrived in May 1900, serving a region that produced wool, wheat, cattle and sheep. The railway also built the Columbia Southern Hotel in 1900–1902. Beyond lodging, it served as a bank, saloon, stagecoach stop and dance hall. Traffic shifted to the Deschutes canyon rail route in 1911, beginning Shaniko’s decline. The hotel remains the town’s most imposing structure, a physical reminder of its shipping role. Shaniko occupies a high plateau of sagebrush, bunchgrass and occasional junipers.

moments.title: Fossil
moments.text: Fossil began as the name of a post office on Thomas Benton Hoover’s ranch in 1876. Hoover chose it after finding fossils in a clay-like rock formation there. In 1881, he and Thomas Watson opened a store near Butte and Cottonwood creeks and moved the post office into it. The connection between town and fossils extends to a public fossil field behind Wheeler High School, where finds include Metasequoia plants. Eighteen miles west along OR 218, the Clarno Unit of John Day Fossil Beds National Monument preserves another part of this fossil landscape.

moments.title: Kam Wah Chung & Co. Museum
moments.text: Ing Hay and Lung On made a former trading post in John Day into a clinic, general store and social center. The two Chinese immigrants bought the business in 1887. Hay asked that the building pass to the city on condition that it become a museum. After his death in 1952, it remained abandoned, and the city’s ownership was forgotten until a park survey in 1967. The city began restoring its 1940s appearance and also holds company records and the proprietors’ personal documents. The museum preserves a Chinese herbal apothecary and mercantile establishment from the post-Civil War West.
